subject: biology
topic: Risk factors, correlation and scatter diagrams
about: Gradify's own explanations, written for the knowledge engine (2026-11-25); draft until a specialist reviews them. The datasets are illustrative, made up for practice, and say so wherever they are shown: they are not real measurements and must never be presented as such.

items.title: Risk factors
items.text: A **risk factor** is anything linked to an increased chance of developing a disease. It can be an aspect of a person's lifestyle, such as smoking or diet, or a substance in their body or environment.
items.summary: A risk factor is linked to an increased chance of developing a disease.
examples: Smoking is a risk factor for lung cancer and cardiovascular disease.
Being obese increases the chance of developing Type 2 diabetes.

terms.definition: Something linked to an increased chance of developing a disease

items.title: Correlation
items.text: Two variables are **correlated** when they tend to change together. In a **positive correlation**, as one increases the other tends to increase too; in a **negative correlation**, as one increases the other tends to decrease. The closer the points on a scatter diagram lie to a straight line, the stronger the correlation.
items.summary: A correlation is a pattern of two variables changing together: positive or negative, strong or weak.

terms.definition: A relationship in which two variables tend to change together
As one variable increases, the other tends to increase
As one variable increases, the other tends to decrease

forms.text: Two variables are **correlated** when they vary together. The strength of a linear correlation is measured by a correlation coefficient, from −1 (perfect negative) through 0 (none) to +1 (perfect positive); a significance test then asks whether a coefficient that size could have arisen by chance in a sample of that size.

terms.definition: A number from −1 to +1 measuring the strength and direction of a linear relationship

items.title: Using a scatter diagram
items.text: A scatter diagram shows whether two variables are correlated.
steps: Plot one variable on each axis, each with a sensible, evenly spaced scale and a label with units.
Plot each pair of values as a point; don't join the points up.
If there's a trend, draw a straight line of best fit with about as many points above it as below.
Describe the pattern: positive, negative or no correlation, and how strong it is.
Use the line to estimate values between your measurements.

items.title: Correlation doesn't prove cause
items.text: A correlation doesn't show that one variable causes the other. Both could be caused by a third factor, or the link could be chance. A risk factor is shown to cause a disease only when scientists find a causal mechanism: how one leads to the other.
items.summary: A correlation alone doesn't prove cause; a causal mechanism does.
examples: A causal mechanism is known for smoking and lung cancer: chemicals in tobacco smoke damage the DNA of lung cells.

terms.definition: The process by which one factor brings about another

items.title: Waist size and blood pressure
items.text: A health survey recorded the waist circumference and systolic blood pressure of 12 adults. High blood pressure is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

causation.statement: These data show that a larger waist causes higher blood pressure.
causation.why: They show a correlation only. A third factor, such as diet or lack of exercise, could raise both; showing cause needs a causal mechanism.

steps: As waist circumference increases, blood pressure tends to increase: a positive correlation.
The points lie close to a straight line, so the correlation is strong.
The data alone don't show that a larger waist causes higher blood pressure.

items.title: Exercise and resting heart rate
items.text: A group of 10 adults recorded the hours of exercise they did each week and their resting heart rate.
steps: As weekly exercise increases, resting heart rate tends to decrease: a negative correlation.
The points lie close to a line, so it is strong.

visual.title: Exercise and resting heart rate (illustrative data)
visual.caption: Illustrative data for practice, not real measurements. The points fall from left to right: a strong negative correlation.
visual.alt: A scatter diagram of resting heart rate against hours of exercise per week for 10 people, from 0 to 7 hours. The points fall from about 82 to 62 beats per minute, close to a dashed line of best fit.
description: x-axis: exercise per week, 0 to 7 hours.
y-axis: resting heart rate, about 60 to 85 beats per minute.
Ten points falling from left to right, close to a line: a strong negative correlation.

items.summary: Points falling close to a line show a strong negative correlation.

items.title: Correlation isn't cause
items.wrong: A strong correlation proves that one variable causes the other.
items.right: A correlation shows only that the variables change together; a third factor or chance could explain it. Cause needs a mechanism.

items.title: A line of best fit doesn't join the dots
items.wrong: A line of best fit should go through every point.
items.right: A line of best fit shows the overall trend: it passes as close as possible to the points, with about as many above it as below.

items.title: A few odd points don't cancel a trend
items.wrong: If a few points don't fit the pattern, there is no correlation.
items.right: A correlation is about the overall trend. A few points off the line make it weaker, not absent; check whether they are anomalies.
